A1-A2.headline: How We Make Electricity Using Tiny Atoms

pages.text: Nuclear power makes light and heat by splitting tiny atoms inside big plants. Small units also run space ships far from Earth. This clean power makes very little bad gas compared to coal and oil.
pages.caption: The Leibstadt Nuclear Power Plant in Switzerland

evidence.articleCaption: The Leibstadt Nuclear Power Plant in Switzerland

pages.text: Nuclear power grew fast in the 1970s and 1980s. Big accidents at Three Mile Island, Chernobyl, and Fukushima brought fear and strict rules. Today, it still gives 9 percent of world power, with new plants in Asia.
pages.caption: The town of Pripyat abandoned since 1986, with the Chernobyl plant and the Chernobyl New Safe Confinement arch in the distance

evidence.fileTitle: File:Центр города Припять на фоне 4 энергоблокаа ЧАЭС.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The town of Pripyat abandoned since 1986, with the Chernobyl plant and the Chernobyl New Safe Confinement arch in the distance

pages.text: Fans of nuclear power say it sends out no warm gas while running. It also causes far fewer deaths than dirty coal or gas air. Critics still worry about high costs and bad rays from fuel.
pages.caption: Anti-nuclear protest near nuclear waste disposal centre at Gorleben in northern Germany

evidence.articleCaption: Anti-nuclear protest near nuclear waste disposal centre at Gorleben in northern Germany

pages.text: Many modern plants grew from 1950s U.S. Navy ship engines. Workers dig up special rock and press it into small fuel pieces in metal bars. Safe heat turns water into steam that turns power wheels.
pages.caption: The Ikata Nuclear Power Plant, a pressurized water reactor that cools by using a secondary coolant heat exchanger with a large body of water, an alternative cooling approach to large cooling towers

evidence.articleCaption: The Ikata Nuclear Power Plant, a pressurized water reactor that cools by using a secondary coolant heat exchanger with a large body of water, an alternative cooling approach to large cooling towers

pages.text: Used nuclear fuel stays hot and harmful for a very long time. Countries must cool and store this waste with great care. Leaders now close old plants while testing newer, safer clean power designs.
pages.caption: The nuclear fuel cycle begins when uranium is mined, enriched, and manufactured into nuclear fuel (1), which is delivered to a nuclear power plant. B1-B2.headline: Unlocking The Potential Of Global Nuclear Energy Systems

pages.text: Nuclear power makes electricity from atomic reactions, mainly by splitting uranium atoms in large plants. Smaller units also power space probes. Together, they offer a low-carbon choice alongside fossil fuels.
pages.caption: The Leibstadt Nuclear Power Plant in Switzerland

evidence.articleCaption: The Leibstadt Nuclear Power Plant in Switzerland

pages.text: World output grew fast in the 1970s and 1980s to 300 gigawatts by 1990. Accidents at Three Mile Island, Chernobyl, and Fukushima brought strong debate and tighter rules. Today, nuclear still supplies nine percent of global power.
pages.caption: The town of Pripyat abandoned since 1986, with the Chernobyl plant and the Chernobyl New Safe Confinement arch in the distance

evidence.fileTitle: File:Центр города Припять на фоне 4 энергоблокаа ЧАЭС.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The town of Pripyat abandoned since 1986, with the Chernobyl plant and the Chernobyl New Safe Confinement arch in the distance

pages.text: Supporters point to zero greenhouse gas during daily use and very low death rates compared with coal and gas air pollution. Critics still warn about radiation risks and high building costs.
pages.caption: Anti-nuclear protest near nuclear waste disposal centre at Gorleben in northern Germany

evidence.articleCaption: Anti-nuclear protest near nuclear waste disposal centre at Gorleben in northern Germany

pages.text: Modern plants grew from 1950s U.S. Navy water reactors made for submarines. The fuel path moves from mining uranium to small pellets inside metal rods. Controlled heat makes steam that drives power turbines.

C1-C2.headline: Navigating The Paradox Of Nuclear Energy In A Warming World

pages.text: Nuclear power generates electricity primarily through controlled uranium fission within utility-scale installations, while compact radioisotope units sustain deep-space probes as a low-carbon alternative to fossil fuels.
pages.caption: The Leibstadt Nuclear Power Plant in Switzerland

evidence.articleCaption: The Leibstadt Nuclear Power Plant in Switzerland

pages.text: After expanding to 300 gigawatts by 1990, severe incidents at Three Mile Island, Chernobyl, and Fukushima sparked public opposition and stricter oversight; nevertheless, reactors still supply nine percent of global power.
pages.caption: The town of Pripyat abandoned since 1986, with the Chernobyl plant and the Chernobyl New Safe Confinement arch in the distance

evidence.fileTitle: File:Центр города Припять на фоне 4 энергоблокаа ЧАЭС.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The town of Pripyat abandoned since 1986, with the Chernobyl plant and the Chernobyl New Safe Confinement arch in the distance

pages.text: Proponents highlight negligible operational greenhouse emissions alongside extraordinarily low mortality rates per energy unit relative to fossil particulates, whereas critics underscore radiological hazards and steep capital costs.
pages.caption: Anti-nuclear protest near nuclear waste disposal centre at Gorleben in northern Germany

evidence.articleCaption: Anti-nuclear protest near nuclear waste disposal centre at Gorleben in northern Germany

pages.text: Commercial fleets originated from 1950s U.S. Navy pressurized-water submarine propulsion. The fuel cycle spans uranium mining, enrichment, and ceramic pellets stacked in rods driving sustained chain reactions and steam turbines.
pages.caption: The Ikata Nuclear Power Plant, a pressurized water reactor that cools by using a secondary coolant heat exchanger with a large body of water, an alternative cooling approach to large cooling towers

evidence.articleCaption: The Ikata Nuclear Power Plant, a pressurized water reactor that cools by using a secondary coolant heat exchanger with a large body of water, an alternative cooling approach to large cooling towers

pages.text: Long-term sequestration of high-level spent radioactive fuel—demanding prolonged cooling and secure isolation—persists as a central challenge while states balance retiring aging reactors against next-generation low-carbon designs.
